linkedin.text:
Every August we get calls about upstairs rooms that won't cool down, and the AC is rarely the real problem. More than ten years on Portland metro roofs has taught us that a poorly ventilated attic bakes the living space below it and cooks the shingles from underneath, aging a roof years ahead of schedule.

The mechanics are simple: cool air enters low through soffit vents, warms, rises, and exits near the ridge. Both halves matter. In our inspections, soffit vents blocked by insulation cause ventilation failures as often as missing exhaust does. Our standard recommendation is a ridge vent paired with clear soffit intake: even airflow across the entire attic, no moving parts, and a strict rule against mixing exhaust types, which short-circuits the loop.

The part homeowners are glad to hear: ventilation can usually be corrected on an existing roof in decent condition. This carousel covers the vent types we compare on real Oregon homes and why ridge vents win.

gmb: If your upstairs rooms feel like an oven this August, your attic ventilation may be the reason. A poorly vented attic bakes in summer heat, making top floors hard to cool and aging shingles from below years ahead of schedule. Healthy ventilation is a simple loop: cool air enters low through soffit vents, warms in the attic, and exits high near the ridge. Both halves have to work, and in our inspections, soffit vents blocked by insulation cause problems as often as missing exhaust vents do. Our standard recommendation is a ridge vent, which exhausts evenly along the whole roof line with no motors or moving parts, paired with clear soffit intake. Ventilation can often be corrected without replacing the roof, whether that means clearing blocked soffits, adding intake, or cutting in a ridge vent.
